text:
Philip Rubin holds a BA in psychology and linguistics from Brandeis University (1971) and a PhD in experimental psychology from the University of Connecticut (1975). His research integrates computational, engineering, linguistic, physiological, and psychological methods to study embodied cognition, focusing particularly on the biological foundations of speech and language.
His work in speech technology began in the early 1970s, involving contributions to the ARPANET Network Voice Protocol and digitized speech. At Haskins Laboratories, Rubin was instrumental in designing computational models such as ASY (Haskins articulatory synthesis program) and SWS (Haskins sinewave synthesis program). He designed and implemented methods for describing and controlling articulatory events, known as speech gestures, and co-developed the CASY model. Rubin is also recognized for his theoretical contributions, such as introducing a dynamical systems/action theory perspective on speech, and for his leadership roles in science policy, including serving as Director of the Division of Behavioral and Cognitive Sciences at the National Science Foundation from 2000 to 2003.
